newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch "hands-on" science centre breaks new ground.
newsitem.headline: Dutch "hands-on" science centre breaks new ground.

text.p: Amsterdam, famed for its 17th century architecture and art, strode into the future on Wednesday with the opening of its New Metropolis science centre -- billed as the most advanced in Europe.

Opening its doors to the public after a gala inauguration by Queen Beatrix on Tuesday night, New Metropolis is expected to draw up to 700,000 visitors annually with a hands-on approach to global modern technology.
"We are looked upon as the prototype for the so-called fourth generation of science and technology centres," says New Metropolis director Joost Douma.
Rather than illustrating basic principles to foster what Douma calls "scientific literacy", New Metropolis focuses on the skills required to cope with today's high-tech environment.

As such the 90 million guilder ($46.2 million) project has attracted substantial private sector investment, with some 20 million guilders funded by manufacturing and services sector giants such as Shell, Dutch PTT, Philips and IBM. The remainder has come from central and local government.

By examining the role of technology in society and the changing job requirements prompted by scientific advances, New Metropolis goes one step further than its counterparts elsewhere in Europe, Douma says.
"In setting up these exhibits we worked together closely with other science centres in for example London and Munich, and they're all looking with interest to see how we fare," he says.

Visitors to this futuristic science centre are encouraged to tap into one of the 220 work-stations dispersed over its five themed sections to play sophisticated simulation games, conduct experiments or design new production and transport processes.
"It's not a top-down educational approach, but one of co-design," explains Douma. "Instead of visitors, New Metropolis will have users who change the exhibits as they work with them."
Each of the five theme zones are built around a range of interactive scenarios involving hands-on role play.

The first zone, 'Interactions', deals with the exchange of information, money and goods. Here users can load virtual wallets and play the capital and commodities markets in a trade game designed to lay bare the dynamics of the global economy.
They can also log on for a sophisticated game of on-line 'happy families', approaching others on the network or using video-conferencing facilities to obtain information.

In the technology zone, users are asked to modify the output of a production line to meet the needs of a particular customer, while other zones deal with energy -- how it is produced, converted and distributed -- and scientific experimentation.
Perhaps the most visually impressive is the zone dealing with human nature, which centres on a dream sequence triggered by walking across a touch-sensitive floor.
The sensation is one of walking on water with silhouettes of ever-more agitated swimmers moving below.
Seated at computer terminals around the central display, users can complete tasks designed to give them a greater insight into their own personalities and human nature in general.
"There are tasks dealing with intuition and receptiveness to types of learning," says Douma. "But there's also a quiz to help you gauge your qualities as a lover."
Designed by Renzo Piano, the prize-winning Italian architect of the Pompidou Centre in Paris, the purpose-built building is shaped like an ocean liner.
Its distinctive silhouette noses into the water in Amsterdam's eastern dockside area alongside the maritime museum, a walk away from the city's central station.
"It's intended as an extension to the city, which is why we opted for 'polis' in the name," explains Douma.
In keeping with this function, the centre incorporates a number of freely accessible public squares including a panoramic roof-top terrace and even a job information centre.
At the same time the name also sparks associations with Fritz Lang's 1927 movie epic "Metropolis", an apocalyptic vision of technology run riot, enslaving its users.
"The reference is intentional," says Douma. "But ours is an upbeat vision of the enabling power of technology -- that's why we've called it New Metropolis".
($ = 1.948 Dutch Guilders)
